articles.title: Sofar gains control, safer recovery and better support
articles.dek: Five connected changes turn the solar integration into a more manageable system without sacrificing its recorded energy history.
body: Home Assistant’s Sofar integration can now switch an inverter’s remote on/off control, capture privacy-redacted diagnostics and be pointed to a new network address without deleting the integration. The reconfigure flow preserves entity customizations and history, then verifies the inverter serial number so an entry cannot silently move to a different device.

The same work protects cumulative energy totals during startup. Sofar now restores each total sensor’s prior high-water mark before the first poll, closing a gap in which a torn first read could permanently step a total backward. Diagnostics include the raw register blocks and polled components needed to investigate missing or incorrect readings, while explicitly removing the serial number from both named and raw data.
The series also brought the integration under Home Assistant’s strict-typing checks. Its diagnostics documentation supports the implementation rather than standing as a separate story.
articles.continuity: A coordinated Sofar series adds controls and diagnostics while protecting existing history.

articles.title: ESPHome actions can finally explain their inputs
articles.dek: Descriptions and examples now travel from device YAML to Home Assistant, replacing bare fields with forms that tell people what to enter.
body: ESPHome user-defined API actions previously reached Home Assistant as a name and a set of typed inputs. Brandon Harvey added optional descriptions for actions and descriptions plus examples for each variable, while keeping the existing shorthand configuration valid.

The firmware cost is opt-in: unchanged configurations compile identically, while metadata is included only when declared. The implementation also accounts for the tighter ESP8266 memory model, and was tested on physical ESP8266 and ESP32-C3 hardware.

A companion aioesphomeapi change carries the new fields into Python clients and defaults them to empty strings for older devices. It is Harvey’s first merged contribution to aioesphomeapi—welcome, Brandon.
articles.continuity: The firmware and Python client changes carry the same descriptive metadata end to end.

articles.title: Bluetooth devices stop disappearing between scan modes
articles.dek: A cross-library repair preserves discoveries during active/passive transitions and closes two failure paths that could make devices unreachable.
body: Bluetooth scanning in Home Assistant’s shared libraries now restores known discoveries immediately after an adapter flips between active and passive mode. Bleak 3 clears its seen-device map on every start; the in-place mode switch had not restored it, leaving connection attempts blind until each device happened to advertise again.

Passive scans also recognize more real-world discoverability flag values, and diagnostics now distinguish a device remembered in history from one currently cached by a scanner. A separate fix stops the final retry from selecting passive mode on Linux adapters that do not support it.
That last repair is Radek Podgorny’s first merge in Bluetooth-Devices/habluetooth. Welcome, Radek.
articles.continuity: Several library-level fixes close related discovery and adapter-mode gaps.

articles.title: Elgato lights put power-up behavior and firmware in Home Assistant
articles.dek: New controls decide how lights return after an outage, expose signal health and install firmware without making local control depend on Elgato’s servers.
body: Home Assistant can now choose whether a supported Elgato light restores its last state or uses configured defaults after power returns. Franck Nijhof added controls for default brightness and color temperature, using each device’s own range, plus diagnostic Wi-Fi signal sensors.

A new update entity can find, install and report progress for firmware images distributed inside Elgato Control Center archives. The remote catalog has its own twice-daily coordinator; if Elgato’s server is unavailable, every locally controlled light entity continues to load and operate.
The underlying color-temperature refactor and companion documentation complete a coordinated expansion rather than separate stories.
articles.continuity: Five related implementation changes and their documentation expand one device family together.

pullRequests.title: Add Elgato default brightness and color temperature

articles.title: Modern Forms Gen4 fans expose the fixtures they actually have
articles.dek: Home Assistant now handles separate uplights and downlights, adds color-temperature control and offers a software restart when a fan wedges.
body: Modern Forms Gen4 fans can carry several independently addressable light fixtures, but Home Assistant previously created one light entity and silently left the others unreachable. Brian Towles changed the integration to create one entity per fixture while preserving established identifiers for earlier fan generations.

Gen4 fixtures now advertise their individual color-temperature ranges. Unsupported sleep-timer and adaptive-learning entities no longer appear as inert controls, and actions a Gen4 fan cannot perform return an error instead of false success.
A restart button gives every supported generation a lower-friction recovery step before cutting mains power; the documentation includes that troubleshooting path.
articles.continuity: A four-part Gen4 series makes multiple fixtures and recovery controls reflect the physical fan.

articles.title: Shelly enhanced security no longer forces HTTPS
articles.dek: A first-time contributor fixes a setup assumption for older devices upgraded to Shelly firmware 2.0.
body: Home Assistant had treated Shelly’s enhanced-security setting as proof that HTTPS was enabled and replaced the configured port with the default HTTPS port. That holds for newer factory-provisioned products, but not for every older device updated over the air.

A fix from burmistrzak now respects the supplied port, supporting stricter certificate validation over an explicitly configured connection instead of making the device unreachable. The companion documentation clarifies the distinction between enhanced security and HTTPS.
This is burmistrzak’s first merged contribution to both home-assistant/core and home-assistant.io. Welcome!
